title: The Fear of the LORD and the Voice in the Street
summary: The book opens with a title and a statement of purpose: these proverbs are meant to give wisdom to the simple and the young and to add learning to the wise, beginning with the fear of the LORD. A father then warns his son not to join a gang that ambushes the innocent for plunder, and Wisdom, pictured as a woman, cries out in the city streets, warning those who refuse her that they will reap what they chose.
story: Proverbs 1 is the doorway to the book and to the Old Testament's wisdom writings. The Bible's story so far has been told mostly through events: creation, the exodus, the kingdom of David and Solomon. Here the focus turns to the daily life of an ordinary young person in that kingdom. The title ties the book to Solomon, whom 1 Kings 3 and 4 remember as the king who asked God for wisdom and received it. The chapter sets up the choice that governs the first nine chapters: two voices calling to the young, one inviting him into easy money through violence, the other inviting him to wisdom and life.
historical:
The heading names Solomon son of David, king of Israel, who reigned in the tenth century BC and was remembered for his wisdom and his thousands of proverbs (1 Kings 4:32). The book itself shows that it grew over time, with later headings for sayings copied by King Hezekiah's scribes around 700 BC and for sages named Agur and Lemuel. Many scholars think chapters 1 to 9, with their longer poems, were composed or arranged as an introduction to the older collections, possibly late in the monarchy or after the exile; others see no reason to separate them from the Solomonic tradition. Either way, the prologue in verses 1 to 7 reads as a preface to the whole book, not to chapter 1 alone.

The father's warning about bandits reflects real conditions. In a land without police forces, roads between towns were exposed, and gangs could waylay travelers for their goods. The promise “we will fill our houses with plunder” (verse 13) was the pitch of every band of robbers, and the young men they recruited were exactly the audience this book addresses.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, wisdom was taught in the household and at court, and instruction was commonly framed as a father speaking to his son. Egyptian teaching texts use the same form. Proverbs keeps it but adds something: the mother's teaching is honored alongside the father's (verse 8), and the goal is not only success but righteousness, justice, and fairness before the LORD. A garland on the head and a pendant around the neck (verse 9) were marks of honor and beauty, the way a medal or a wedding ring signals something about the wearer.

The places where Wisdom speaks matter. The street, the public square, the main concourse, and the city gates were the busiest spaces in an ancient town. At the gate, elders heard legal cases, merchants traded, and news was exchanged. Wisdom isn't hidden in a temple or a school; she speaks where ordinary business happens, and she speaks loudly. Sheol and the Pit (verse 12) are the Hebrew names for the realm of the dead, the grave pictured as a mouth that swallows the living.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 7 form a prologue: a title, a long sentence listing the book's purposes, and a motto in verse 7 that functions as the thesis for the whole book. Verses 8 to 19 are the first of the father's instruction speeches, each opening with my son, and include a quoted speech by the gang whose words are turned against them: they lie in wait for blood but end up ambushing their own lives. Verses 20 to 33 give the first speech of Wisdom personified, which sounds like a prophet's oracle: a call, an accusation, a warning of judgment, and a closing promise. The chapter introduces the book's cast of characters: the simple (naive and open to influence), the fool (settled in folly), and the scoffer (who mocks correction).

outline.t: Title, purpose, and motto: the fear of the LORD
Listen to your father and mother
Refuse the invitation of violent men
Wisdom cries out in the streets

doctrines.note: The chapter defines biblical wisdom: skill in living rightly, which includes righteousness, justice, and fairness, and which begins with the fear of the LORD. Wisdom is moral and religious before it is practical, and it can be refused.
Parents are the first teachers of wisdom, and the mother's teaching stands alongside the father's. The home is pictured as the place where a young person learns to see the world rightly.

The gang's plan shows how sin works: it promises gain and companionship, but greed destroys the ones who pursue it. Those who reject wisdom finally eat the fruit of their own way. Sin carries its own consequences within it.

words.note: Mashal, proverb. The word covers short sayings, comparisons, parables, taunts, and even longer poems. Its root idea is likeness or comparison: a proverb sets one thing beside another so that a pattern in life becomes visible. That tells us how to read the book: as observations about how life generally works, not as legal rules or guaranteed outcomes.

Yirah, fear. In verse 7 and verse 29 it describes the fear of the LORD, which in the Old Testament means reverence, awe, and trust toward God that shows itself in obedience. It is not panic, but it is not less than a sober recognition that God is God and we are not. Proverbs calls this the beginning, the first principle and starting point, of knowledge.

Peti, the simple. The word describes someone naive, inexperienced, and easily persuaded, open in the sense of a door that anyone can walk through. The simple aren't yet fools; they can go either way. That is why both the gang and Wisdom call to them, and why the book is addressed to them.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter directly, but it picks up its themes. Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Jesus spoke of wisdom being justified by her deeds (Matthew 11:19), identifying his own ministry with wisdom's call. Wisdom's cry, “How long, O simple ones, will you love your simple ways?” (verse 22), finds an echo in Jesus's lament over Jerusalem, where he longed to gather its children and they were not willing (Matthew 23:37). The link is thematic rather than predictive: the chapter pictures wisdom calling publicly and being refused, and the Gospels show Jesus doing the same in the streets and towns of Galilee and Judea.

hard.q: Does Wisdom really laugh at people's disasters and refuse to answer when they finally call?
hard.a: Verses 26 to 28 are hard to read. Wisdom says she will mock the calamity of those who refused her and will not answer when they seek her. Two things help. First, this is poetry in the style of a prophetic warning, and the point is the seriousness of the choice: there comes a point when consequences arrive and can't be undone, and those who scorned counsel for years can't summon it instantly in a crisis. The mocking reverses the scoffers' own mockery (verse 22). Second, the speech is addressed to those who persistently refuse, and it is spoken now, while there is still time; its purpose is to turn hearers before the storm comes. Wisdom's outstretched hand (verse 24) shows the invitation was real. The rest of Scripture shows God welcoming the repentant, but it also warns that delay is dangerous. Verse 33 describes the usual outcome of listening, safety and security, as a pattern of life under God rather than a promise that the wise never suffer, a question the books of Job and Ecclesiastes take up directly.

questions: What voices in your life, like the gang in verses 11 to 14, promise quick gain or belonging if you will just go along?
What does it mean to you that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, rather than something added after you have figured things out?
Wisdom speaks in the busiest public places. Where in your ordinary day might wisdom be calling, if you were listening?
